title: Human-AI Ensembles in Mergers and Acquisitions
abstract: Organizations increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI) in strategic decision domains once governed entirely by human judgment. Mergers and acquisitions (M&As)—rare, heterogeneous, and causally ambiguous events—represent a setting in which traditional, human-only learning systems repeatedly fail to convert experience into improved performance. We theorize how hu-man–AI (H–AI) ensembles, in which human and artificial agents jointly generate and aggregate judgments, reconfigure the mechanisms of organizational learning in M&As. Building on be-havioural perspectives of learning, we develop a process model of hybrid intelligence that ex-plains how ensembles create, transfer, and retain experiential knowledge through the combina-tion of codified algorithmic pattern recognition and human interpretive reasoning. We show how ensemble architectures reshape the applicability, accessibility, and adoption contingencies that govern the experience–performance relationship, thereby addressing long-standing puzzles about why acquisition experience so often fails to yield superior outcomes. By conceptualizing H–AI ensembles as learning architectures rather than decision aids, our theory enriches organi-zational learning with a technology-conscious account of how hybrid systems accumulate, pre-serve, and deploy experiential knowledge in complex strategic contexts. This perspective also broadens research on AI in management by illustrating how hybrid intelligence alters the condi-tions under which organizations learn from rare, high-stakes decisions.

title: Combining monolingual and multilingual training for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer in XTREME-R
abstract: Intermediate-task training---fine-tuning a pretrained model on an intermediate task before fine-tuning again on the target task---often improves model performance substantially on language understanding tasks in monolingual English settings. We investigate whether English intermediate-task training is still helpful on non-English target tasks. Using nine intermediate language-understanding tasks, we evaluate intermediate-task transfer in a zero-shot cross-lingual setting on the XTREME benchmark. We see large improvements from intermediate training on the BUCC and Tatoeba sentence retrieval tas Research goal: What is the impact of combining both monolingual English and multilingual intermediate-task training on zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance in the XTREME-R benchmark? title: PRIVACY-PRESERVING AUTONOMOUS SYSTEM ROUTING VIA INTELLIGENT GRAPH FILTERING
abstract: Traditional inter-domain routing protocols' decentralized architecture can cause a number of problems, such as misconfiguration and convergence problems. Alternative strategies that use the Software Defined Networking (SDN) paradigm to give more control over routing operations have been put forth recently in response to these issues. In this scenario, an SDN controller is assigned to handle routing duties in a multidomain network made up of Autonomous Systems (ASs). Each controller must learn how to connect to any node outside of its domain in order to carry out inter-domain routing. Because the controllers must access sensitive, business-critical data (such link charges) across all domains, serious privacy issues arise. In order to preserve privacy, protocols for determining the shortest path between a source and a destination a typical policy in routing tasks have recently been presented. These protocols rely on MultiParty Computation (MPC) techniques, which limit scalability by ensuring anonymity at the expense of high computational and communication complexity. In this study, we use Data Mining (DM) approaches to eliminate nodes that have a low probability of being reached by the shortest path, thus pruning the network graph. On the pruned graph, privacy-preserving shortest path methods are then conducted at a significantly reduced complexity.

title: Temporal-consistency Replay SMOTE: A Historical Trajectory Oversampling Method via Temporal-consistency Replay Mechanism
abstract: Class imbalance is a prevalent challenge in the analysis of historical trajectory data within domains such as the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), Internet of Vehicles (IoV), and smart grids. Traditional Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) and its variants primarily focus on static feature spaces, which often destroy the temporal continuity and physical consistency of trajectory data when performing linear interpolation. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel oversampling algorithm named Temporal-consistency Replay SMOTE (TCR-SMOTE). The proposed algorithm introduces a temporal-consistency replay mechanism to synthesize virtual trajectory samples. First, asynchronous minority trajectories are projected and realigned onto a standardized replay timeline using cubic spline interpolation. Second, a dynamic control factor based on kinematic similarity is designed to adaptively guide the spatial interpolation process. Finally, a consistency correction operator integrating first-order physical motion equations is applied to adjust the synthesized spatial coordinates, ensuring that the velocity and acceleration conform to realistic physical laws. The TCR-SMOTE algorithm guarantees that the generated virtual trajectories are not only spatially representative but also highly realistic in their temporal evolution, providing an effective and high-fidelity data augmentation solution for imbalanced trajectory classification.
